strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear critique of layer-wise REM limitations (Section 2)
Strong empirical results achieving 7.8× perplexity improvement at 90% sparsity across multiple models (125M-27B)
Principled optimization approach grounded in ADMM theory with convergence proofs for both ELSA and ELSA-L
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple architectures (OPT, Gemma, LLaMA), scales, and evaluation metrics including perplexity and zero-shot tasks
Practical scalability via ELSA-L with 66% memory reduction, enabling 27B model pruning
Useful ablations demonstrating the importance of objective-aware projection (Table 3) and comparing NTP vs. REM (Figure 6)
Consistent improvements over 8 baseline methods across diverse models and sparsity levels
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—ADMM is standard (Boyd et al., 2011), Hessian-weighted pruning dates to OBS (LeCun et al., 1989), and Fisher-diagonal approximation is well-established; contribution is primarily the combination

Computational cost inadequately addressed: no wall-clock time, FLOPs, or computational comparison provided despite 4,096 iterative training steps required; unclear if performance gains justify cost vs. one-shot baselines
Hyperparameter sensitivity with high heterogeneity across models (learning rates: 1e-5 to 2e-1, penalty λ: 1e-4 to 1e-2, different schedules); no clear guidance for practitioners on new models
Weak convergence guarantees: only convergence to λ-stationary points (not global optima), complex conditions in Theorem 4.6, no empirical convergence analysis, and strong bounded iterates assumption

Experimental reproducibility concerns: baseline hyperparameter selection unspecified, unusual results in Table 6 (NaN values, values reaching 1.6e4 suggesting instability), no error bars or statistical significance testing, single runs only
Data requirements underspecified: calibration set sizes not clearly stated, Figure 6 shows NTP requires more data than REM at low regimes with unclear practical implications
Memory advantage claims (Section 6) not empirically validated; comparison with layer-wise methods' actual memory usage is missing despite being central to motivation
No actual inference benchmarks: reports perplexity/accuracy but not inference speedup, latency, or deployment-time memory usage—critical for practitioners
Limited novelty in objective-aware projection (Section 3.2): unclear why Diag(H) is preferable to full Hessian; Fisher-weighted magnitude pruning not compared as simpler alternative
Limited analysis of extreme sparsity ceiling: why does performance max at 90%? What prevents higher sparsity? Not addressed

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification: clearly articulates three fundamental limitations of layer-wise reconstruction approaches that are compelling and well-presented
Impressive empirical results: achieves 90% sparsity across multiple architectures (OPT, Gemma, LLaMA) with consistent 5-30× improvements in perplexity over state-of-the-art at high sparsity
Strong downstream task performance: maintains 6.06%p average accuracy advantage at 90% sparsity across 7 zero-shot tasks, demonstrating robust generalization
Solid theoretical grounding: provides rigorous convergence analysis for both ELSA and ELSA-L with proper treatment of quantization effects in the proofs
Technical innovations: objective-aware projection using Fisher information is clever, well-motivated, and efficiently leverages existing optimizer states from Adam
Comprehensive experimental validation: covers multiple scales (125M-27B), architectures, sparsity levels (50-90%), and adaptations to different sparsity patterns (N:M, non-uniform)
Scalability demonstrated: ELSA-L enables pruning at 27B scale with 66% memory footprint reduction, showing practical applicability to larger models
Thorough ablations: demonstrate value of both objective choice (NTP vs REM) and objective-aware projection, with gains increasing at higher sparsity levels
weaknesses: Missing practical efficiency metrics: no wall-clock time comparisons during pruning despite ADMM requiring 4096 iterative steps; no actual inference latency/throughput measurements on hardware

Hyperparameter selection lacks guidance: Table 5 shows dramatic variation in learning rates (1e-5 to 2e-1) and penalties across models; no principled approach for selecting hyperparameters for new models or limited sensitivity analysis

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: identifies why layer-wise fails but provides limited insight into why surrogate-free formulation specifically enables 90% sparsity versus other possible mechanisms
Weak theoretical guarantees: convergence to λ-stationary points only, not global optima; no characterization of solution quality relative to other methods or sample complexity analysis

Inconsistent moderate-sparsity performance: ELSA sometimes underperforms at 50-60% sparsity (Table 6: OPT-1.3B 50% is 19.66 vs 16.38 for SAFE); insufficient explanation of this trade-off and when to use ELSA
Limited ablation of technical choices: diagonal Hessian approximation is aggressive but alternatives not explored; ablation only tests projection on/off rather than different variants
Scope limitations: all experiments on transformer LLMs only; generalization to RNNs, MoE models, diffusion models unclear; evaluation limited to primarily English next-token prediction
Defensive memory analysis: discussion argues layer-wise methods don't save memory but lacks concrete numerical comparisons; memory claims may be overstated
Incomplete non-uniform analysis: Table 2 only compares evolutionary methods at 70% sparsity; finding that uniform ELSA beats optimized non-uniform allocation deserves deeper investigation
Opaque computational cost: practical pruning time compared to one-shot baselines is unclear despite claimed efficiency advantages

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem analysis: Excellent diagnosis of layer-wise method limitations through equations (1) vs (2), identifying three specific pitfalls that are convincing and well-articulated

Principled methodology: Direct optimization of true sparsity-constrained problem via ADMM is theoretically grounded; objective-aware projection using Fisher information is elegant and leverages existing optimizer states without additional cost

Breakthrough empirical results: Demonstrates consistent ability to achieve 80-90% sparsity while maintaining model quality across multiple architectures (OPT, Gemma-2, LLaMA-2/3) and scales (125M-27B), clearly breaking through the previously observed 'sparsity wall'

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple evaluation metrics (perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, inference speed, memory), strong baselines (7 methods), detailed numerical results, and proper ablation studies demonstrate technical rigor
Theoretical contributions: Convergence guarantees for both ELSA and ELSA-L with quantization, grounded in optimization theory with formal proofs
Scalability demonstration: ELSA-L successfully prunes 27B models with 55% reduced memory footprint, showing practical viability at large scales
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Well-written paper with clear visualizations, detailed experimental settings in appendices, and commitment to releasing code
weaknesses: Significant computational cost: ELSA requires ~1.78 GPU-hours on 4×A100 at 90% sparsity versus 0.16h for Wanda (~7-11× more expensive); cost-quality trade-off analysis is brief and unclear when this investment is justified, limiting practical adoption

Complex and model-dependent hyperparameter tuning: Tables 5-6 show learning rates and penalty parameters vary significantly across models and sparsity levels with no principled guidance; raises reproducibility concerns and suggests substantial engineering effort was required

Unfair experimental comparison: Baselines use 128 calibration sequences while ELSA uses 32,768 data points, confounding the comparison. While justified as necessary for iterative optimization, it's unclear whether baselines would improve substantially with more data—this should be better controlled

Limited analysis of why the method works: Paper identifies problems with layer-wise methods but doesn't deeply explain why surrogate-free formulation specifically overcomes them. What sparse structures does ELSA find that differ from competitors? Is the landscape fundamentally different? This limits understanding of applicability

Hardware dependency not addressed: Inference speedup measured only with MACKO kernel on RTX 3090; practical benefits entirely depend on availability of specialized sparse kernels in production systems, which is glossed over

Generalization concerns: Semi-structured (N:M) sparsity results show ELSA is only 'roughly on par' with baselines; non-uniform sparsity shows smaller gains. This suggests advantages are specific to uniform sparsity patterns, limiting applicability
Incomplete ablations: Objective function ablation only at OPT-125M 90%; geometric projection ablation only at LLaMA-3.2-3B. More comprehensive ablations across settings would strengthen paper

Weak theoretical guidance for practitioners: Convergence to λ-stationary points (not global optima); condition 'λ chosen large enough so that λ⁻¹β² - (λ - μ)/2 < 0' lacks practical implementation guidance; no sensitivity analysis provided

strengths: Clearly identifies and articulates three specific limitations of existing layer-wise reconstruction error minimization approaches (error compounding, sequential suboptimality, surrogate objective mismatch)
Principled methodological contribution: formulates pruning as proper constrained optimization and solves via ADMM, moving beyond heuristic-based approaches
Dramatic empirical improvements at extreme sparsity: 10-100× better perplexity than baselines at 90% sparsity across all tested models
Comprehensive experimental validation: 6 models (125M-27B), multiple sparsity levels, zero-shot tasks, extreme sparsity (99%), practical speedups (3.98×) and memory savings (7.80×)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating importance of objective choice (NTP vs REM) and objective-aware projection, validating design decisions
Theoretical convergence guarantees provided for both ELSA and ELSA-L, even with quantization
Scalability demonstrated on 27B models with memory-efficient ELSA-L variant (55% memory reduction)
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and code release commitment
weaknesses: Significant computational cost (7.12 GPU-hours on 4× A100s for LLaMA-2-7B at 90%) limits practical adoption; 28-44× more expensive than one-shot methods despite arguing for quality-cost tradeoff
Hyperparameter tuning complexity requires extensive per-model and per-sparsity configuration (learning rates: 5e-5 to 2e-4, λ: 1e-4 to 5e-2, schedule changes); limited guidance for new settings

Limited analysis of why surrogate-free optimization works: unclear whether improvement stems from eliminating surrogate, global joint optimization, or penalty formulation; ablation separating these factors would strengthen claims
Structured sparsity results (N:M patterns) show no advantage over baselines, suggesting method benefits only unstructured sparsity and limiting hardware deployment scenarios
Calibration data requirement (32,768 points) is 256× more than baselines; scaling behavior not thoroughly analyzed
Convergence to λ-stationary points rather than global optima is weaker guarantee for non-convex setting; solution quality assessment missing
Hardware and kernel dependence: inference gains rely on specific MACKO sparse multiplication; results not validated on other sparse kernels or hardware
Modest real-world usability despite perplexity gains: zero-shot accuracy at 90% sparsity (38.52%) remains far below dense (59.67%), raising questions about practical deployment
Baseline comparisons at extreme sparsity (95-99%) limited to Wanda with fine-tuning; matched compute budget comparisons would strengthen claims
